section_summary: This section concludes an account of postwar labor conflict in the Japanese press, emphasizing union divisions, management authority, and the definition of editorial rights. It then presents detailed surveys of Japan’s postwar shortages and allocation of newsprint and other newspaper-production materials. The final pages examine newspaper advertising, circulation, inflation-driven rate increases, advertising ethics, and the opening of an article on cooperative newspaper distribution.

subfiles.title: Post-War Labor Movement
subfiles.about: Continues an analysis of postwar labor disputes, union fragmentation, management authority, and editorial rights in the Japanese newspaper and broadcasting industries.
subfiles.summary: Article on the Yomiuri and Hokkaido Shimbun disputes, the failed general strike, secessions and reunification attempts, management councils, purges, the Nishi Nippon Shimbun dispute and publishers' principles on editorial rights.
keywords: All-Japan Press and Radio Workers Union

subfiles.title: Japan's Newsprint
subfiles.about: Surveys wartime and postwar newsprint production, shortages, controls, allocation policies, public-opinion polling, and prospects for recovery.
subfiles.summary: Ishimitsu attributes the collapse of newsprint production to coal and transportation shortages, the loss of Sakhalin pulp supplies, and the reduction or conversion of paper mills. He traces wartime newspaper consolidation and newsprint control, followed by the gradual transfer of allocation authority to civilian bodies after the surrender. The article describes newspaper cooperation, the 1947 readership survey, production reorganization, proposed increases in paper size, and the Clearing House Society’s effort to align circulation and allocations with reader choice.

subfiles.title: Existing Conditions of Other Materials
subfiles.about: Reviews shortages, rationing, and distribution problems affecting materials and utilities required for newspaper production.
subfiles.summary: Taneda: newspapers depended on rationed or black-market supplies; sections on ink, metals, paper, textiles, coal, rubber, chemicals and electricity show persistent shortages despite imports and intervention.

subfiles.title: Newspaper Advertising in Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes the scale, economics, organization, and ethical regulation of newspaper advertising in postwar Japan.
subfiles.summary: Nishibe argues that newspapers were Japan’s dominant advertising medium because commercial radio did not exist and magazine circulation was constrained by paper controls. Statistical tables document newspaper circulation, steep inflation-driven increases in advertising rates, subscription charges, and the differing dependence of national, provincial, economic, evening, and newly founded papers on advertising income. The article also reviews advertising categories and agencies, calls for ethical purification after deceptive advertisements contributed to a Tokyo infant-death scandal, and advocates circulation auditing through the American A.B.C. system.

subfiles.title: The Newspaper Cooperative Distribution Association, Its Past, Present, and Future
subfiles.about: Begins a report on the organization and reach of Japan’s cooperative newspaper-distribution system.
subfiles.summary: Newspaper Cooperative Distribution Association, a juridical person from December 1, 1946; 110 of 149 dailies joined, 17.8 million copies or 97 percent of output; begins listing offices.
